meaning: A model or policy that conditions on visual observations and language and produces robot actions or an action representation for embodied control.
guidance: Specify all inputs, the action space, control frequency, training data, and whether actions are generated directly, discretized as tokens, or decoded by a separate head.
avoid: Do not call a vision-language model a VLA merely because its textual output can be interpreted by an external planner.
examples: The VLA policy maps camera observations and a language instruction to a sequence of robot actions.
We fine-tune the pretrained VLA on {number} demonstrations from {target embodiment}.

provenance.note: Independent definition synthesized across open, cross-embodiment, and 3D VLA papers.

meaning: A control policy whose action prediction depends jointly on sensory observations and a linguistic task specification or instruction.
guidance: State the language granularity, observation modalities, action horizon, and whether language changes the task, goal, or low-level behavior.
avoid: Do not imply compositional language understanding unless it is evaluated under an appropriate held-out split.
examples: The language-conditioned policy predicts actions from {camera views}, proprioception, and the instruction.
We evaluate whether the policy follows unseen combinations of familiar language concepts.

provenance.note: Field-standard terminology indexed from generalist robot-policy and multimodal-prompt work.

meaning: A representation that maps continuous or structured robot controls into discrete tokens or token-like outputs for sequence-model prediction.
guidance: Describe discretization bins, dimensions, control semantics, decoding, clipping, and any embodiment-specific normalization.
avoid: Do not assume that language-token and action-token probabilities have the same semantics or that tokenization is lossless.
examples: Each action dimension is discretized into {number} bins and represented by a dedicated token range.
The predicted action tokens are decoded into {control command} at {frequency} Hz.

provenance.note: Technical terminology indexed from RT-X and OpenVLA action-generation formulations.

meaning: Predicting a block of consecutive future actions in one policy inference step rather than predicting only the next action.
guidance: Report chunk length, execution or replanning frequency, overlap between chunks, and whether observations are incorporated again before the entire chunk is executed.
avoid: Do not equate action chunking with open-loop execution; implementations may replan or aggregate overlapping chunks.
examples: The policy predicts a chunk of {k} future actions from the current observations.
We replan every {n} control steps and combine overlapping action chunks with {aggregation rule}.

provenance.note: Independent definition based on action-chunk prediction in ACT and sequence prediction in visuomotor policies.

expression: separate prediction horizon, execution horizon, and feedback frequency
meaning: A policy may predict many future actions while executing only part of them before receiving a new observation, so action horizon alone does not determine whether control is open-loop or closed-loop.
guidance: Report all three quantities and explain how overlapping predictions are combined. Use 'closed-loop' only when updated observations influence subsequent executed actions.
avoid: Do not infer the control-feedback structure solely from the number of actions output by the network.
examples: Although the policy predicts {k} actions, it replans after executing {n}, using a new observation.
The controller executes the entire chunk open-loop before the next policy query.

provenance.note: Independent reporting guidance synthesized from chunked and diffusion-based action policies.

expression: temporal ensembling of overlapping action predictions
meaning: Combining action predictions made at different policy-query times for the same future control step.
guidance: Describe the weighting function, overlap window, and whether aggregation occurs in action space or another representation. Mark ACT-specific weighting choices as implementation details rather than universal definitions.
avoid: Do not confuse temporal ensembling with an ensemble of independently trained policies.
examples: At each control step, we aggregate overlapping action predictions using exponentially decaying weights.
Temporal ensembling smooths predictions from successive action chunks.

provenance.note: Method terminology indexed from ACT and generalized only at the level of overlapping action predictions.

meaning: Manipulation in which two robot arms or end effectors must act in a coordinated manner to accomplish a task.
guidance: Specify whether coordination is symmetric or asymmetric, the control space for each arm, sensing, synchronization, and the task phase requiring coordination.
avoid: Do not call independent single-arm subtasks bimanual coordination unless their actions are coupled by the object or objective.
examples: The benchmark contains contact-rich bimanual tasks that require coordinated motion of both end effectors.
The policy jointly predicts left- and right-arm actions at {frequency} Hz.

provenance.note: Independent definition grounded in the bimanual manipulation setting studied by ACT.

meaning: A robot trajectory collected while a human operator controls the robot through a physical, graphical, wearable, or other remote interface.
guidance: Report the interface, observation available to the operator, control rate, filtering, intervention policy, and whether unsuccessful attempts are retained.
avoid: Do not use 'human demonstration' without distinguishing robot teleoperation from videos or state–action data generated outside the target robot.
examples: We collect {number} teleoperated demonstrations with a leader–follower interface.
The dataset retains both successful and unsuccessful teleoperation episodes.

provenance.note: Field-standard data-collection terminology indexed from ALOHA and DROID.

meaning: A training collection that combines trajectories from multiple robot platforms, embodiments, institutions, tasks, or data-generation pipelines.
guidance: Report contributing datasets, sampling weights, action and observation normalization, license or availability constraints, and the target platforms used for evaluation.
avoid: Do not equate a large aggregate trajectory count with balanced coverage across robots or tasks.
examples: We pretrain on a cross-robot mixture and fine-tune on demonstrations from the target embodiment.
The mixture sampling weights are chosen by {rule} rather than in proportion to raw dataset size.

provenance.note: Independent definition synthesized from Open X-Embodiment, Octo, and OpenVLA.

expression: heterogeneous robot action spaces require an explicit alignment strategy
meaning: Different datasets and embodiments may use controls with different dimensions, frames, grippers, rates, and semantics, so joint training requires a documented representation or adapter.
guidance: Specify coordinate frames, normalization, missing dimensions, embodiment identifiers, and decoding into each robot's native controller.
avoid: Do not describe actions as standardized when only file formats are shared but control semantics remain different.
examples: We map each dataset's controls into a common {representation} and retain an embodiment-specific action mask.
Actions are normalized per embodiment before joint training and decoded with {adapter}.

provenance.note: Independent implementation guidance synthesized from cross-embodiment policy and dataset work.

meaning: A task specification composed of more than one modality, such as interleaved text, images, object crops, goals, or demonstrations.
guidance: List the modalities, tokenization, temporal order, and information available at test time. Distinguish a prompt that specifies a task from observations generated while executing it.
avoid: Do not call ordinary multimodal observations a task prompt unless they communicate the intended task or goal.
examples: The prompt interleaves a language instruction with images of the target objects.
We evaluate novel compositions of visual and textual prompt elements.

provenance.note: Independent definition based on multimodal prompt specification in VIMA.

meaning: A language-model-based system that directly incorporates continuous or encoded sensor modalities to support reasoning or prediction grounded in an embodied environment.
guidance: Specify the sensor encoders, how their outputs enter the language model, the training tasks, and whether the system predicts language, plans, values, or executable actions.
avoid: Do not assume that multimodal grounding alone makes the model a closed-loop robot controller.
examples: The embodied language model interleaves visual and state-estimation embeddings with text tokens.
The model supports {planning or question answering}, while a separate controller executes robot actions.

provenance.note: Independent definition based on the embodied language-model formulation in PaLM-E.

expression: distinguish VLA policies from embodied language models
meaning: A VLA label emphasizes action generation for control, whereas an embodied language model may use sensor inputs for reasoning or prediction without directly producing executable actions.
guidance: Classify a method by its actual output and control interface rather than model backbone. Some systems may satisfy both descriptions, but the overlap should be stated.
avoid: Do not use VLA, vision-language model, and embodied language model interchangeably.
examples: Unlike embodied language models evaluated on reasoning tasks, our VLA directly predicts {robot control representation}.
The model supplies high-level plans to a separate low-level policy and is therefore not evaluated as an end-to-end VLA controller.

provenance.note: Independent terminology boundary synthesized from PaLM-E and OpenVLA.

meaning: In 3D-VLA, a model that uses 3D scene information and language-conditioned representations to generate future scene or action-related predictions for embodied manipulation.
guidance: Attribute this formulation to the specific paper and describe its generated variables. Do not present the phrase as a universally standardized VLA architecture.
avoid: Do not infer that every 3D-grounded VLA is a world model or that every world model predicts robot actions.
examples: Following {source}, we use '3D VLA world model' for a model that predicts {paper-specific outputs}.
Our system differs because it predicts {actions only or future observations only}.

provenance.note: Paper-specific terminology boundary independently paraphrased from 3D-VLA.

expression: evaluate embodied generalization along separately controlled axes
meaning: Systematic evaluation varies identified factors—such as objects, placements, task templates, prompt compositions, environments, or embodiments—while documenting which combinations were withheld.
guidance: Define each split procedurally and report results by axis. Use 'zero-shot' only when the evaluated factor or combination was absent from training under the stated protocol.
avoid: Do not collapse all held-out conditions into one generalization score that hides qualitatively different shifts.
examples: We report separate results for unseen objects, unseen task compositions, and unseen embodiments.
The hardest split holds out both {factor one} and {factor two} during training.

provenance.note: Independent evaluation guidance synthesized from multimodal-prompt and cross-embodiment studies.

meaning: The fraction or percentage of evaluation trials that satisfy a predefined task-completion criterion.
guidance: Define the success criterion, trial unit, number of trials, aggregation level, and treatment of partial completion and timeouts. Provide uncertainty where appropriate.
avoid: Do not compare success rates computed with different horizons, reset policies, human interventions, or success detectors without qualification.
examples: Task success rate is computed over {number} independent trials using {completion criterion}.
The policy succeeds in {count}/{total} trials, corresponding to {percentage}%.

provenance.note: Field-standard evaluation terminology indexed from manipulation and VLA papers.
